{{short description|Fictional legislation}}
{{Good article}}
The '''Metallic Metals Act''' was a fictional piece of legislation included in a 1947 American opinion survey conducted by Sam Gill and published in the March 14, 1947, issue of ''Tide'' magazine. When given four possible replies, 70% of respondents claimed to have an opinion on the act. It has become a classic example of the risks of meaningless responses to [[closed-ended question]]s and prompted the study of the pseudo-opinion phenomenon.

==The question==
Respondents were asked this question and were given four possible answers: "Which of the following statements most closely coincides with your opinion of the Metallic Metals Act?"<ref name="mystery text"/>

* It would be a good move on the part of the [[United States|US]]
* It would be a good thing, but should be [[States' rights|left to the individual states]]
* It's alright for foreign countries, but should not be required here
* It is of no value at all

==Initial publication and reaction==
Sam Gill was a Marketing Research Director for Sherman & Marquette, Inc when he included a question about the fictional Metallic Metals Act in a survey. He reported on the results in the March 14, 1947, issue of ''Tide'' magazine in an article titled "How Do You Stand on Sin?", saying that 70% of respondents claimed to have an opinion on the topic.<ref name="Bishop">{{cite book |last=Bishop |first=George F. |date=2005 |title=The Illusion of Public Opinion |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fpzrs-bSD3gC&q=%22Metallic+Metals+Act%22&pg=PA19 |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |page=19 |isbn= 9780742516458 }}</ref><ref name="Payne"/> Gill also asked respondents if they favored [[incest]], an unfamiliar term to most people at the time, and one third supported it.<ref name="mystery text"/> The article did not include any information on the size or make-up of the [[Sample (statistics)|sample population]], nor how much pressure the interviewer applied to receive a response.<ref name="comedy">{{cite web |url=https://io9.gizmodo.com/the-metallic-metals-act-shows-people-always-bluffed-abo-1582877203 |title=The Metallic Metals Act Shows People Always Bluffed About Politics |last=Inglis-Arkell |first=Esther |date=June 6, 2014 |website=[[IGN]] |access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref>

A similar study by Eugene Hartley in 1946 asked college students how connected they felt to students of various nationalities. His questionnaire included three imaginary nationalities, but a majority of students did not question them.<ref name="mystery text"/> Together, these two studies are the earliest publicized examples of opinion surveys on fake subjects, a phenomenon known as a '''pseudo-opinion'''.<ref name="Bishop2"/><ref name="Bishop 3"/> At the time, the results of both studies amused [[laymen]] but were not immediately taken seriously in the field of public opinion because most professionals felt the studies were ridiculous and reflected negatively on their field.<ref name="Payne">{{cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=Stanley L. |title=Thoughts About Meaningless Questions |journal=The Public Opinion Quarterly |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=687–696 |jstor=2746245 |year=1950 |doi=10.1086/266248 }}</ref> One exception, Stanley L. Payne, wrote about Gill's study in the 1951 ''[[The Public Opinion Quarterly]]'' journal article "Thoughts About Meaningless Questions" and called for further investigation into this type of [[non-sampling error]].<ref name="Payne"/>

==Legacy==
Despite Payne's call to action, pseudo-opinions remained largely unstudied until the 1980s,<ref name="Bishop 3">{{cite journal |last1=Bishop |first1=G. |last2= Oldendick |first2=R. |last3=Tuchfarber |first3=A. |last4=Bennett |first4=S. |date=1980 |title=Pseudo-Opinions on Public Affairs |journal=The Public Opinion Quarterly |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=198 |doi=10.1086/268584 |jstor=2748428 }}</ref> but in 1970 Philip Converse postulated that answering "don't know" is seen by respondents as an admission of "mental incapacity".<ref name="Shuman">{{cite book |last1=Schuman |first1=Howard  |last2=Presser |first2=Stanley |date=1996 |title=Questions and Answers in Attitude Surveys |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Je640UKqNaYC&q=%22metallic+metals+act%22&pg=PA147 |publisher=Sage |page=147 |isbn= 9780761903598 }}</ref> In 1981, researchers Howard Schuman and Stanley Presser were unable to locate documentation for Gill's study and concluded it should be taken as an [[anecdote]] rather than a true study.<ref name="Bishop2">{{cite journal |last1=Bishop |first1=G. |last2=Tuchfarber |first2=A.|last3=Oldendick|first3=R.|date=1986 |title=Opinions on Fictitious Issues: The Pressure to Answer Survey Questions |journal=The Public Opinion Quarterly |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=240 |doi=10.1086/268978 |jstor=2748887 }}</ref> Their research found that pseudo-opinions are a significant source of error but not as prevalent as Hartley and Gill's studies suggested.<ref name="mystery text">"[https://courses.eller.arizona.edu/mgmt/delaney/p_chapter5.pdf How Questions Affect Answers]" p55. Retrieved July 17, 2018</ref>

The Metallic Metals Act is considered a classic example of pseudo-opinions and difficulties with close-ended survey questions<ref name="Bishop"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Lawless |first1=Harry T. |first2=Hildegarde |last2= Heymann |date=August 31, 1999 |title=Sensory Evaluation of Food |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BTR7VEJPDWAC&q=%22metallic+metals+act%22&pg=PA511 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |page=511 |isbn=9780834217522 }}</ref> and continues to be supported by later studies.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2015/12/18/political-ignorance-and-bombing-agrabah/?noredirect=on |title=Political ignorance and bombing Agrabah |last=Somin |first=Ilya |date=December 18, 2015 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> By 1991, it had become standard practice to include a false question in opinion surveys to gauge the degree of pseudo-opinions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Baker |first1=Michael J. |date=1991 |title=Research for Marketing  |chapter=Data collection — questionnaire design |publisher=Palgrave |location = London |pages=132–158 |doi=10.1007/978-1-349-21230-9_7| isbn=978-0-333-47021-3 }}</ref> A study by the University of Cincinnati found 20 to 40 percent of Americans will provide pseudo-opinions because of social pressure, using context clues to select an answer they believe will please the questioner.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.kivitv.com/-/the-bomb-agrabah-survey-shows-how-problematic-polling-can-be |title=The 'Bomb Agrabah' Survey Shows How Problematic Polling Can Be |last=Daniels |first=Eugene |date=December 18, 2015 |website=[[KIVI-TV]] |access-date=July 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180718234655/https://www.kivitv.com/-/the-bomb-agrabah-survey-shows-how-problematic-polling-can-be |archive-date=July 18, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> This has occasionally provided a source for jokes on [[talk show]]s and comedy shows who air interviews to mock the respondents.<ref name="comedy"/> Other studies have shown the phenomenon is not limited to the United States.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2015/05/23/survey-suggests-that-one-third-of-us-8th-graders-believe-that-canada-france-and-australia-are-dictatorships/ |title=Survey suggests that one third of US 8th graders believe that Canada, France, and Australia are dictatorships |last=Somin |first=Ilya |date=May 23, 2015 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date= July 17, 2018}}</ref> In a 2019 opinion piece written for ''[[The Guardian]]'', [[Richard Seymour (21st-century writer)|Richard Seymour]] speculated that most opinion polls represent only what respondents heard most recently in the news media.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2019/sep/20/polls-public-opinion-polling-industry|title=The Polling Industry Doesn't Measure Public Opinion - It Produces It|last=Seymour|first=Richard|author-link=Richard Seymour (21st-century writer)|website=The Guardian|date=September 20, 2019|access-date=February 20, 2020}}</ref>
